_meta.model: claude-haiku-4-5-20251001 (MODELS.FAST), 1 route / two states (log, review patterns)
_meta.why_v2: Ground-up rebuild (commit 622372be) replaced the six-mode weekly-audit design (Daily Check-In, Planner, Recharge, Weekly Audit, Say Yes?, Journal — capacity/budget arithmetic, cost-per-hour math, weekly_budget/recovery_time sections) with two states: log one interaction, review patterns across logs. The v1 cases below (main-audit, week-planner, quick-check, recharge-minimal) tested endpoints (/plan, /quick-check, /recharge) and fields (energy_score, drains, rechargers, weekly_budget) that no longer exist and were replaced wholesale. This re-record was overdue — golden went unrecorded at v2's own rebuild and was failing 0/4 by the time this correction pass found it.
_meta.why_v2_1: Owner review of live output found the pattern-reasoning engine overclaiming beyond the data in five ways: (1) converting a contrast between two logs into an implied cause ('something about the pace or dynamic differed') instead of naming every candidate feature and saying the log doesn't establish which mattered; (2) statistical-sounding language ('does not predict') from a 3-entry sample; (3) test_next experiments that changed more than one variable at once (or, once fixed, asked the visitor to wait for a deliberately MISMATCHED combination of two conditions to break a confound — still a compound ask); (4) energy-transfer language ('cost'/'added'/'reduced') for what is only a before/after self-rating, not a battery measurement; (5) calling a 2-4-observation split a 'pattern' before the evidence actually earned that word. CONTRACT gained a CONTRAST DISCIPLINE section, a rewritten PATTERN THRESHOLD with an explicit evidence-count ladder and a banned-word list (predict/predicts/predictive/predictor; pattern below 5 comparable observations), and an ACTION section requiring single-variable experiments with a mandatory fallback (track one variable across future ordinary logs, never a manufactured or deliberately-mismatched next interaction) when the candidate variables are confounded in the supplied logs. Frontend: the 'My patterns (N)' tab was renamed 'What I'm noticing (N)' across all 13 languages — the tool has observations and contrasts at this stage, not yet repeated comparable observations, so 'patterns' overclaimed its own confidence.
_meta.how_to_regression_diff: Re-run cases (npm run check:golden sea). Diff for QUALITY not exact match: HTTP 200, no truncation. GUARDS: validateResult() in backend/routes/social-battery-advisor.js keys on summary.headline/body being present; caps worth_noticing<=3, contrasts<=2, not_enough_to_tell<=4; forces test_next to one well-shaped object; summary.counts is always recomputed in code from the actual submitted logs, never trusted from the model. The five epistemic corrections above are prompt-enforced (CONTRACT), not code-checkable — when eyeballing new captures, grep the JSON for 'predict', 'pattern' (below 5 comparable observations), 'cost'/'drained'/'restored'/'added energy', and read every test_next.experiment for a second named variable or a compound wait-for condition. DO NOT reverse: the array caps, the recomputed counts, or any of the five CONTRACT disciplines above.

logs.note: Six people. I knew everyone, but the conversation moved fast.
Small group and I mostly listened.
We talked for about half an hour.

summary.headline: Three interactions produced different outcomes: one ended lower, one unchanged, one higher.
summary.body: The dinner with six people where you felt a lot on ended 2 points lower. The team meeting where you felt some on ended unchanged. The call with your sister where you felt not much on ended 2 points higher.

worth_noticing.title: On-ness and energy outcome did not line up consistently
worth_noticing.evidence: The dinner log shows high on-ness (a_lot) ending lower (4→2). The sister call shows low on-ness (not_much) ending higher (2→4). The team meeting shows medium on-ness (some) ending unchanged (3→3).
worth_noticing.meaning: Across these three entries, feeling more on did not consistently go with lower energy afterward, and feeling less on did not consistently go with higher energy. With only three entries and three different outcomes, this makes on-ness worth continuing to track rather than treating as an explanation yet.

worth_noticing.title: Group size and energy outcome are separate questions
worth_noticing.evidence: The dinner was six people and ended lower (4→2). The team meeting was small and ended unchanged (3→3). The call was one person and ended higher (2→4).
worth_noticing.meaning: In these three entries, smaller groups did not consistently end higher or lower — the one-on-one call ended higher while the small team meeting ended unchanged. Too few entries to settle what matters about group size.

contrasts.title: Dinner (ended lower) vs. sister call (ended higher)
contrasts.first: Dinner with six people, high on-ness, ended 4→2
contrasts.second: Phone call with sister, low on-ness, ended 2→4
contrasts.question: Several features differed between these two: group size (six vs. one), on-ness (a_lot vs. not_much), and likely duration and setting as well. This log does not tell you which of these differences, if any, mattered to the opposite outcomes.

test_next.observation: The dinner and sister call produced opposite results, and on-ness differed between them. It is worth testing whether on-ness itself matters, separate from the other things that also differed.
test_next.experiment: Over your next several interactions, pay attention to how on you felt regardless of who you were with or how many people were there. Comparing on-ness to your energy outcome across more entries, independent of group size, will help separate the two and show whether one of them matters more than the other.
test_next.watch_for: Does higher on-ness consistently go with lower energy after, or does it vary like it did in these first three logs?

not_enough_to_tell: Whether on-ness itself drives the energy change, or whether group size, duration, familiarity, conversation pace, or another feature is what matters
Whether the same interaction would produce the same result next time
What role the starting energy level (before the interaction) plays in the outcome

logs.note: About 25 relatives, lots of small talk.
Big crowded room, many new people.

summary.headline: Large group interactions ended lower; small group interactions ended higher.
summary.body: The three interactions with 20+ people and high on-ness all ended 2-3 points lower in energy. The two interactions with one other person and low on-ness both ended 2 points higher. Group size and on-ness moved together in every log, making it unclear which one, if either, explains the difference.

worth_noticing.title: Large crowded interactions ended lower; one-on-one interactions ended higher.
worth_noticing.evidence: Work happy hour (20+ people, a_lot on-ness, 4→2), family reunion (25 people, a_lot on-ness, 4→1), and networking mixer (crowded room, a_lot on-ness, 3→1) all ended lower. Coffee with close friend (two people, not_much on-ness, 3→5) and walk with neighbor (two people, not_much on-ness, 2→4) both ended higher.
worth_noticing.meaning: These two groups had opposite outcomes in every entry. However, they differ in at least two ways: group size and how much you felt you had to be on. The logs do not yet show which of these matters, or whether both do.

contrasts.title: Large group with high on-ness ended lower; one-on-one with low on-ness ended higher.
contrasts.first: Work happy hour: 20+ people, a_lot on-ness, energy ended at 2
contrasts.second: Coffee with close friend: two people, not_much on-ness, energy ended at 5
contrasts.question: These differ in group size, on-ness, familiarity (close friend vs. coworkers), setting (loud bar vs. quiet coffee), and duration. This log does not tell you which of these, if any, explained the opposite outcomes.

test_next.observation: Group size and on-ness moved together in all five logs — larger groups came with higher on-ness, smaller groups with lower on-ness. To separate these two, watch for how on you feel across your next several logs, regardless of group size or setting.
test_next.experiment: Over your next several interactions, notice how much you felt you had to be on, independent of whether the group was large or small. Log as usual. Comparing on-ness to energy outcome across more entries — setting aside group size for now — will help show whether on-ness alone tracks with your energy change.
test_next.watch_for: Does higher on-ness tend to match lower ending energy across different group sizes, or does the relationship depend on group size too?

not_enough_to_tell: Whether group size or on-ness (or both, or neither) actually explains the energy changes.
How duration, setting, or familiarity contributed to the outcomes.
What will happen in a large group where you feel less on, or a small group where you feel more on.

logs.note: I feel like I am heading toward a bigger crash, not just tired from this one call.

summary.headline: One interaction ended notably lower in energy.
summary.body: Back-to-back client calls left you at energy 1, down from 3. You felt a lot on during the calls. Your note mentions concern about heading toward a bigger crash rather than simple fatigue from this session alone.

worth_noticing.title: Energy ended notably lower after feeling a lot on during back-to-back calls.
worth_noticing.evidence: This single entry: energy changed from 3 to 1 (a drop of 2 points), with on-ness marked as a_lot.
worth_noticing.meaning: This one session shows a clear downward shift. With only one log, you cannot yet know whether this outcome is typical for back-to-back calls, typical when on-ness is high, or specific to something else about this particular session — group size, duration, type of call, or something not captured in these fields. Worth continuing to track as more similar interactions occur.

not_enough_to_tell: Whether back-to-back calls themselves tend to lower your energy, or whether high on-ness during calls is what mattered, or whether something specific to this session (content, number of calls, duration, or people involved) drove the result.
What on-ness feels like during interactions that end higher or unchanged, and how that compares to this session.
Whether this energy level is typical for you after similar work, or whether this session was unusual.

handoff.reason: Your note explicitly mentions concern about heading toward a bigger crash, not just fatigue from this one interaction. Before the Crash can help you track whether this is an isolated session or part of a larger pattern building toward overload.
